The reading order starts inside the file: first establish how names enter the file, then see how this file organizes them, and only then connect the external uses whose locations have already been identified.

The initial draft used the word "calls" somewhat broadly. At the time, it recorded only the starting point and a few leads to investigate, making it easy to treat imports, uses within the same file, and consumption outside the module as the same kind of relationship. This revision keeps the title because it is easy to search for; the arrows in the body are separated by relationship type. No arrow is added without a source location.

```text
holidays/calendars/germany_school.py
          |
          +-- Top-level names entering the file
          |
          +-- Declarations and rule expressions in this file
          |
          `-- Located uses outside the module
```

This is not an execution sequence diagram. It lays out the three layers of notes to leave after opening the file. The first layer answers where names come from, the second what they do in this file, and only the third which other locations actually use objects exposed by the module. Mixing the three layers makes an import look, in later searches, like a calendar calculation that has already run.

## Top-level names

Start at the top of `germany_school.py` and log the imported items line by line. Keep the spellings used in the source; do not assign them new Chinese labels. If an imported name later appears in a class definition, rule set, constructor expression, or conditional branch, that location can be appended as a use within the same file. If the notes show only the import line, stop at "enters the file." Both states are common. Do not claim that a name contributes to a result just because it looks like a calendar base class, date utility, or rule constant.

Aliases in particular need their own entries. An alias changes the string used in subsequent searches and can make "where it is imported from" and "where it appears" seem to refer to different names. The notes should retain both the original import location and the location where the alias appears in an expression, rather than recording only the more familiar one. That way, when returning to the file, it is clear where the name changed.

## Declarations in this file

There is no need to copy every syntactic block in the second step. Mark only module-level objects that can be searched for elsewhere, and where they sit relative to rule expressions in this file. If a name is used only to assemble another declaration, it can still help explain the file's internal structure, but should not be listed directly as a module export. Conversely, an object's declaration at module scope alone does not establish that it is used by a package-level entry point or consumer.

Writing in source order is more reliable than following a guessed business flow. For example, if a name first appears in a declaration and is then placed in another expression, that shows the organizational order within the file. Whether it represents a particular school region, when it produces date results, and whether it is combined with other calendars are all questions to leave to the corresponding use sites. These reading notes focus on the links between names and expressions, without filling in explanations of behavior that has not been seen.

For repeated occurrences of the same name, use the first to locate its source and later ones to determine whether it participates in the module's internal structure. If a later occurrence is only in a comment, a string, or a type position, record it separately from places where the name actually participates in an expression. This is not about ranking names, but about keeping search results from mixing textual mentions with code uses. If this comes up during review, append the location after the name; there is no need to rewrite the entire relationship description.

## Arrows beyond the module boundary

The cross-file section accepts only entries with paths. Another file importing an object again shows that the object is passed on to another module. Only when an external location places it in a calendar construction, registration operation, or query expression can the notes go on to describe that specific use. Both are worth recording, but need different arrow labels. Do not label the former "executed the rules," or reduce the latter to "saw the same name."

This page does not assume which directory contains the first consumer of `germany_school.py`. When a reference is found, add the referencing file's path, the source-level name being used, and the enclosing expression to this section. If the search finds only an import, stop the record at that import. That way, someone tracing a caller back to this file later can tell which part is a confirmed connection and which is still only adjacency within the file.

This page collects only name-related leads for `germany_school.py`; when comparing the two modules, retain each one's paths and object names in its own notes.

The initial draft's to-dos have not been treated as completed. The body adds reading targets and ways to describe relationships, rather than filling in a symbol table without source excerpts. The next time someone follows this starting point, the most useful additions will be the original names of module-level objects, the first actual use of each direct import, and the first unambiguous use outside the module. # Bangladesh Holiday Status Decision Record

The original question was not the holiday itself, but whether the naming layer should switch to a different output once a religious date moved from estimated to confirmed. Code around the old implementation treated the date, language, and confirmation status as one thing: whenever the date changed, callers could only reinterpret the entire entry. - Keep name selection independent; make the date/status transition the only point of consolidation.

# Bangladesh Holiday Status Decision Record

The initial version of this page framed the problem too narrowly, as if renaming a confirmed date would be enough. The original passage was retained after review, but we no longer rely on that conclusion. The real risk is folding three things into the same block of generation logic: moving a date from tentative to confirmed, switching from the default name to Bengali, and callers treating a hint in the name as a status field.

Half of the early agreement still holds: callers must not infer confirmation status from the name. The other half needs correcting. At the time, we described "keeping the name unchanged" as an implementation strategy, when it was only an output goal. The actual flow of entries determines whether the generator performs date calculation in one place and whether it selects local names elsewhere.

`islamic_generator.py` remains the first entry point we found. The file header contains `from __future__ import annotations`, `defaultdict`, `timedelta`, and `TYPE_CHECKING`. These dependencies are enough to show that the file assembles date-related objects and retains type-checking branches; they do not establish which object holds the name. The old record directly equated "the file includes islamic" with "the file owns all religious holiday names." That inference has been withdrawn.

## Two proposed approaches

**Option A: Encode confirmation status in the display name.** That way, existing callers do not need to understand a new status concept and can tell from the name whether it might still change. The cost is that the name is no longer just a name; localized output is polluted with a maintenance-oriented hint, and equivalent wording has to be found for each language. If callers sort or compare strings, the hint itself also becomes another source of differences.

**Option B: Update the entry itself once the date is confirmed, and continue selecting the name according to the language rules.** This gives callers a stable name, with confirmation status handled through the date data and the timing of its generation. The cost is that debugging requires checking both the date and the name, rather than just searching for a suffix.

We decided to continue with Option B. "Stable" here does not mean using the same string every year. It means that the same confirmed record does not undergo an extra language change because of the migration steps. It also does not require retroactive changes to historical output generated while dates were still estimates; whether old results included a hint reflects the old version's behavior and is not being changed by this decision.

## Retained earlier proposal

The passage below is the migration approach originally proposed. It has been abandoned and is retained because it explains why people later kept looking for a name suffix.

> For religious dates that are not yet confirmed, append an estimate hint to the name; once confirmed, remove the hint and change the name back to the default language. If no local name is available, keep using the English name.

The problem is "change the name back to the default language." It ties confirmation status to language fallback, so a confirmed date can lose a local name that was otherwise available. That change was rejected. Name fallback is no longer used as a signal that confirmation is complete.

The earlier claim that "keeping the name unchanged is enough" also needs to be narrowed. It only means that display output should not be changed without reason; it does not mean that the estimated and confirmed stages must produce identical text for every source and every year. Date sources can be revised, and name sources may be revised too; what this decision rejects is deliberately making confirmation trigger a fallback to English.

## Check order after a review

During one investigation, a language change in a returned value was attributed to a shift in date calculation. That explanation did not hold up: date calculation and name selection may happen next to each other, but they are not the same decision. The former answers which day; the latter answers what to display for that day. If the date is changed first and the name difference is then used to explain the result, it is easy to mask both problems at once.

The verification order was then changed to two steps: first, check whether the target date has already entered the confirmation path; then, check which name that entry gets in the selected language. Both checks are required; neither can replace the other. When the date is not the confirmed date, even a name that looks exactly like the final local name is not enough to show that the migration is complete; when the date is already confirmed, an extra estimate hint in the name cannot be treated as normal display output either.

This adjustment did not introduce any new public parameters. Existing consumers mainly look up the calendar by date; adding a field to expose an internal migration would turn a fix scoped to one data source into an interface change. If a caller genuinely needs to distinguish tentative from confirmed in the future, a separate proposal should be made for representing status, rather than stuffing hint text into the holiday display name.

## Review notes

One comment left in review was: "Look for a counterexample first. If a confirmed record can still be labeled with two different statuses depending on the language selected, then it is not a naming problem." This later became the standard for the checks here. The counterexample we need is not more samples from other countries, but a case where the same Bangladesh entry is still affected by the old hint after confirmation.

Another comment asked that Bangladesh's handling not be generalized into a uniform rule for all Islamic holidays. That restriction remains. The generation path includes date shifts and grouping, but the available material does not support applying a single migration strategy to every country, every language, or every religious source.

## Decision at this stage

- Confirmed dates do not carry estimate hints in their display names.
- When a local name is available, confirmation status must not force it to fall back to the default language.
- Check date confirmation and name selection separately; if the former is not established, the latter's result cannot be used as evidence of confirmation.
- Do not add caller-facing fields that serve only this migration.

An unanswered question is whether local names in the estimated stage should be exactly the same as in the confirmed stage, or whether different names supplied by the sources themselves are allowed. Another question is whether old query results preserved the entries generated at the time. The existing records are not enough to define a backfill strategy for either question; when a specific discrepancy comes up, first distinguish historical results from a regenerated calendar.

# Bangladesh Holiday Status Decision Record

This record has remained tucked between several changes to the religious calendar. It was retained not because Bangladesh has a special date algorithm, but because three different judgments were mixed in over time: treating date confirmation as a display-name change, treating Bengali as a temporary fallback, and treating the generated file as the sole point of ownership. Each made troubleshooting easier at some point, but they cannot all hold true at the same time.

The earliest page recorded only one concern: once a date changed from estimated to confirmed, would callers see the same holiday switch to another language. At the time, no year, specific entry, or interface scope was recorded. This gap later led to two opposing readings: some believed the estimate indicator should be retained until the next release cycle; others believed confirmation should lead directly back to the default English. Both treated the name as a proxy for status.

The additions below remain in the order they were made. The old paragraphs have not been rewritten for consistency; they explain why the current decision is narrower than the earlier agreement, and why a single string change is not enough to conclude that something went wrong in the date path.

## Conventions Left from the Drafting Stage

The early working assumption was that confirmation status belongs to the date source, while the name is a presentation choice. This assumption was not written as an interface rule at the time; it was simply intended to avoid expanding a date revision into a set of name replacements. When an entry moves from estimated to confirmed, the change should first be reflected in whether the date can be used as a definite date; if the name has a local form, it should not lose that local form just because the date has been confirmed.

Appending the estimate indicator directly to the holiday name was considered at the time. The argument in favor was that existing callers were already reading the string and would not need to look elsewhere for status. The objection was that once the string also served as status, translation, sorting, and comparisons of the same holiday would all become ambiguous. A caller seeing an English indicator cannot tell whether it represents the date source, a missing translation, or a local convention in a particular region.

The initial decision therefore favored separation: the name should not carry confirmation status. But that decision did not specify whether different language names could be used in the estimated and confirmed stages, nor did it specify how to fall back when an unknown language was encountered after confirmation. It only ruled out the shortcut of "replacing the local name with the default English".

The early wording included the sentence "It is enough to leave the name unchanged". This sentence was later crossed out, but not deleted. At the time, it was shorthand for stability for callers, not a requirement for every data source, every language, or every year to produce identical text. Whether the names match still depends on the calendar names and language selection available at the time; that shorthand cannot be read as mandatory equivalence across sources.

That version also left behind an incorrect shortcut assumption: as long as the indicator after the name disappeared, the date must be usable. This was not retained as a troubleshooting rule later. The indicator comes from the presentation strategy, whereas whether the date enters the confirmed path is determined by entry generation; the two may appear in the same change, but they are not the same fact.

## Annotations Beside the File Entry Point

Earlier troubleshooting linked the issue name and the call name to `scripts/calendar/islamic_generator.py`. This entry point is still retained here because it is one of the first files opened when reviewing religious date generation. The file header shows:

```python
from __future__ import annotations
from collections import defaultdict
from datetime import timedelta
from typing import TYPE_CHECKING
```

These four dependencies leave only partial clues. `defaultdict` indicates that the generation process aggregates objects,`timedelta` indicates that date shifting takes place within it, and `TYPE_CHECKING` indicates that type relationships may be handled outside runtime. None of them can replace inspection of the final entries, much less establish that all name selection is completed here.

One version of the investigation notes once called this file the "owner of religious holiday names". That label no longer applies. The generator's involvement in organizing date objects does not mean that it alone determines every localized display name, every language fallback, or every country-specific alias. At this stage we still treat it as a navigation entry point: follow the adjacency relationships in entry generation to find confirmed dates and names, rather than infer implementation ownership directly from the filename.

This correction also changes the order in which differences are examined. The previous habit was to look for strings first, then ask why the date had changed. Now the order is reversed: first check whether the target date is estimated or confirmed, then look at the name attached to that date. If the date is not confirmed, no matter how much the name looks like the final localized name, it is not enough to show that the migration is complete; if the date is already confirmed, an additional estimate notice in the name likewise cannot be treated as normal display content.

The date utilities in the file header only indicate a link to date shifting here, and do not justify attributing the confirmation status of a given day to the shifting itself. Objects used for aggregation are not the same as objects used for language selection either. This side note is retained to prevent later readers from assigning responsibility for an output difference to a single file based solely on the import list.

## Old Migration Draft (Retained)

The following approach was included in an intermediate draft, but was not adopted later:

1. Append a notice to the name for estimated dates.
2. Remove the notice when the date is confirmed.
3. At the same time replace non-English names with the default English names, so callers do not read different languages across two release cycles.
4. If callers need localized names, have the callers translate them themselves.

The third step is the problem. It ties "confirmation" and "English names" together as a single action, effectively treating localization as unreliable decoration. For Bangladesh, this would cause entries that already have Bengali names to lose their original wording just as their dates become more reliable. Worse still, callers can only infer the internal state from name changes, and cannot distinguish whether the cause is a confirmation migration, a change in language settings, or a source revision.

This draft has been discarded, and is retained not so that subsequent implementations follow its steps for compatibility, but to explain why the old proposal to "switch to English after confirmation" occasionally appears in the material. That was an option that was not adopted, not a commitment about historical behavior.

The fourth step in the draft was not adopted as a processing path either. Having callers translate names themselves may seem to spare the generator from making language decisions, but it would result in the same national calendar having different names for different consumers. This does not establish that all languages must be handled by the same layer; it only means that replacing names with English after confirmation is no longer treated as the default solution.

## The Check Sequence Left Behind by a Misjudgment

During a later review, someone noticed the name change first and attributed the issue to a date offset. That line of reasoning did not hold up. Date calculation and name selection may appear close together along the same generation path, but the former answers which day it is, while the latter answers what is displayed for that day. Treating them as a single error makes it easy to break names while fixing dates, and to obscure the fact that a date remains unconfirmed while filling in names.

A simpler verification procedure was therefore retained.

- First locate the target date in the country calendar and determine whether it is an estimated date or a confirmed date provided by the source.
- Then check name selection for that same date; do not use the presence or absence of a hint in the name as a substitute for the previous step.
- If the language selection can provide a local name, confirming the date must not require falling back to the default language.
- Only when the local name itself has no available value should normal language fallback be considered; this is separate from confirmation status.

This sequence does not require adding a status field. The reason is not that status has no value, but that this revision only addresses the relationship between generation and display for existing calendar entries. Changing the public return shape to make a migration easier to diagnose would expand a fix to a local data source into a migration for callers. If consumers do need stable access to "estimated/confirmed" in the future, status representation and compatibility should be discussed separately; display names must not be used to carry these signals again.

"First locate" here does not mean that the search must start with a filename. You can start from `scripts/calendar/islamic_generator.py`, or trace back from a target date that has already been generated; the key is that the final object being checked is still an entry in the country calendar. If the investigation stops around imports, grouping, or date shifting, it cannot distinguish a date revision from a name revision.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> EstimatedDate
    EstimatedDate --> ConfirmedDate: Date confirmation
    EstimatedDate --> LocalNameSelection: View name
    ConfirmedDate --> LocalNameSelection: View name
    LocalNameSelection --> LocalNameRetained: Name available
    LocalNameSelection --> NormalLanguageFallback: Name unavailable
    LocalNameRetained --> [*]
    NormalLanguageFallback --> [*]
```

The diagram does not make "name available" a condition for confirmation. The two lines leading from date states into name selection are precisely the boundary preserved by this correction: confirmation and language selection must both be checked, but neither can substitute for the other. Normal language fallback remains a branch of name selection, not the endpoint or a failure indicator of the confirmation path.

## Review Excerpts and Subsequent Changes in Wording

One reminder recorded during the review was: "Look for a counterexample first. If a confirmed record can still be described as having two different statuses depending on the language selection, then it is not a naming issue." This statement did not dictate where to implement the change, but it brought the debate back to something that could be checked: the same confirmed date should not be misread as still being at the estimated stage simply because its local name is retained.

Another comment was more specific: do not erase language differences to prove name stability. Stability should mean that an entry under the same language selection carries no unnecessary traces of migration, not that every call must return English, nor that every language has the same translation in every year. This comment corrected the earlier, overly broad statement that "it is enough for the name to remain unchanged."

Another discussion attempted to fold "unknown language" into confirmation handling: since the confirmation date needs to be output explicitly, an unknown language should always return the default name. This was not accepted. Unknown-language fallback is an ordinary branch of name selection; date confirmation only requires the date and entry to have been finalized, and cannot thereby define a cross-language fallback policy. Conflating the two would make future language fixes look like date migrations.

The review did not require extending Bangladesh's handling into a unified rule for all Islamic holidays. The date sources, language support, and confirmation cadence for different countries are not uniformly defined by this record. The generation path includes date shifts and grouping, and there is no basis for consolidating every country, language, or religious source into the same migration strategy.

From this point on, the decision on this page was narrowed to three points: confirmation status is not hidden in the display name; an available local name is not withdrawn because of confirmation; and date confirmation and language fallback are checked separately. It does not replace the rules for other countries or financial calendars, nor does it assign a unique responsibility to every internal object in the generator.

## Early Cases Retained as Background

Two examples appeared in early drafts and were treated as evidence of "generic religious holiday behavior." They are now retained only as historical background.

The first example treated any local script as a temporary value that had not yet been normalized and recommended standardizing it to English after confirmation. This is precisely the third step that was later abandoned. It overlooked the fact that a local name may itself be the calendar's normal external representation, and it did not distinguish whether the name change came from a source revision or a confirmation migration.

The second example treated the hint after the name as the sole source of status and assumed that the disappearance of the hint was enough to assert that the date had been confirmed. This judgment no longer applies. The hint may come from an old display strategy, and the name itself is not a record of the date source. Investigation needs to return to the entry date and confirmation path, rather than only comparing strings.

Neither of these old examples was extended into the current requirements. They remain here because discussions of old calls still refer to phrases such as "standardize to English" or "the hint disappears"; when reading these phrases, it should be understood that they came from approaches that were not adopted. They are not operational instructions retained for compatibility.

Another early opinion held that, since the generator uses `defaultdict`, the language name should be fixed during aggregation. This judgment was likewise not adopted. Aggregation is visible local adjacency and cannot by itself prove at which step the display name was selected. This opinion is retained so that future reviewers know why someone once looked for name differences along the aggregation logic.

## Adjacent Issues Still Not Split Out

One adjacent issue has not yet been split out: if the source first provides a local name and an estimated date, then revises the holiday's translated name during subsequent confirmation, the caller will see the date and name change at the same time. It is not possible here to predetermine which item caused the user-facing difference. The current decision only prohibits deliberately switching to the default language to represent confirmation; it does not prohibit the source from revising the name itself.

Another unresolved point is historical queries. Whether results already generated by an old version should retain the estimated-date hint from that time, or return the current naming rules when regenerated, depends on whether the specific query saved the entry as generated. This page does not contain enough material to define a backfill policy. When this issue arises, first confirm whether the query retrieved a historical result or a regenerated calendar, then decide whether a separate compatibility note is needed.

Outputs for regional aliases, financial calendars, or a subdivision cannot be included in this decision yet. They cover different entities. Even if religious holidays or localized names also appear elsewhere, Bangladesh's confirmation handling must not be reused merely because the strings are similar. This restriction does not deny that they may have similar issues, but prevents a fix for one national calendar from inadvertently becoming a shared rule.

These issues are not included in the current decision because they concern source revisions, historical results, and other calendar scopes, respectively, rather than being restatements of the same output relationship between confirmed dates and Bengali names for Bangladesh. Deciding them all together would make a fix that should be local take on additional interface commitments.

## Current release requirements

Following the revisions above, the current requirements apply only to the two sample dates in the Bangladesh national calendar, with date confirmation, the language of the name, and estimation indicators handled separately: on 2024-02-26, the Bangladesh national calendar uses শবে বরাত to label Shab-e-Barat, and on 2026-05-28 it uses ঈদুল আজহা to label the confirmed Eid al-Adha, and names for confirmed dates must not carry an estimation suffix.

This sentence replaces the part of the old draft that said "revert to the default English after confirmation", not the normal fallback for an unknown language. The first date is retained as a local-name sample, while the second serves as a sample with no remaining signs of estimation once confirmation has been finalized; both must be checked together to avoid fixing only half of the issue.

During implementation review, start with the national calendar as the scope, and do not misread this as a requirement for a financial calendar or a particular subdivision. If the resulting date is correct but the name contains an estimation indicator, revisit the point where the confirmation status is incorporated into the entry; if the date is correct and there is no indicator but the name falls back to English, revisit the branches for language selection and local-name retention. If there is no name in the target language to begin with, follow that language's existing fallback rules, and do not interpret the absence as a confirmation failure.

This requirement applies directly only to the two given dates. It does not require every name at the estimation stage to be exactly the same as at the confirmation stage, nor does it claim that all future holidays will be free of source revisions. What it requires is this: confirmed target dates must not retain the appearance of their previous status through an estimation suffix, nor may they lose an available Bengali name as a result of confirmation.

## How to record changes after the decision

This page no longer recommends describing this type of revision as a "rename". When recording a change, at least make clear what it concerns: date confirmation, a name revision, or a language fallback. All three may appear in the output as a different string, but they involve different maintenance actions.

For changes involving date confirmation, first record the target date and the confirmation result; for name issues, record the selected language and the actual name; for language fallback, record why the local name is unavailable. Records kept this way can explain why a holiday entry changed without forcing readers to infer the internal state from English versus local-language text.

The wording in the previous version about "names remaining unchanged" can still serve as a reference for the intent: do not let the transition to confirmed status needlessly disrupt the display. But it can no longer be used to oppose actual name revisions provided by the source, nor to require all languages to share a single name. The current decision protects the continuity of local names on confirmed dates, as well as the absence of an estimated suffix after confirmation.

## Appendix: Judgments that were previously conflated

- "The presence of Bengali means the date is confirmed." Overturned. Language is the result of name selection, not evidence of confirmation.
- "English is the safest choice after confirmation." Overturned. Defaulting to English is not a way to represent confirmed status.
- "As long as the notice is removed, the date is guaranteed to be usable." Overturned. Whether the date itself has entered the confirmation path must be checked.
- "The generator file determines all output semantics." No longer adopted. This entry point is useful for troubleshooting, but the actual relationship between names and dates should still be verified against the generated entries.

These judgments are not retained to maintain compatibility with them. They are part of this page's history, and also explain why the current requirements specify only two dates, two Bengali name forms, and the confirmation suffix, rather than cramming in all behavior for other countries, other calendar categories, or unknown languages.

For Bangladesh, this would cause entries that already have Bengali names to lose their original expression precisely when their dates become more reliable. Worse, callers could only infer the internal state from name changes, without being able to distinguish a confirmed migration from a language-setting change or a source revision.

This draft is obsolete. It is retained not to require later implementations to remain compatible with its steps, but to explain why the documentation may occasionally contain the old proposal to "change to English after confirmation". That was an option that was not adopted, not a commitment to historical behavior.

The draft's fourth step also did not become part of the processing path. Having callers translate names themselves may seem to avoid making the generator handle language decisions, but it would cause the same country's calendar to have different names for different consumers. This does not prescribe that all languages must be handled at the same layer; it only means that replacing a confirmed name with English is no longer treated as the default solution.

## An inspection order left by a misjudgment

During a later review, someone noticed the name changes first and attributed the issue to a date shift. That line of reasoning did not hold up. Date calculation and name selection can occur close together along the same generation path, but the former answers which day, while the latter answers what to display for that day. Treating them as a single bug makes it easy to break names when fixing dates, and to obscure the fact that a date is still unconfirmed when adding names.

A more straightforward verification method was therefore retained.

- First, locate the target date in the country calendar and check whether it is an estimated date supplied by the source or a confirmed date.
- Then check name selection for that same date; do not use whether the name includes a hint as a substitute for the previous step.
- If the language selection can provide a local name, the confirmation action must not require a fallback to the default language.
- Only if the local name itself has no available value should normal language fallback be discussed; this is separate from confirmation status.

This sequence does not require adding a status field. This is not because status has no value, but because this revision only addresses the relationship between generation and display for existing calendar entries. Changing the public return shape to make a migration easier to diagnose would expand a limited data-source fix into a migration for callers. If consumers do need to reliably read "estimated/confirmed" in the future, status representation and compatibility must be discussed separately; signals must no longer be smuggled into display names.

Here, "locate first" does not mean starting the search with a filename. You can start from `scripts/calendar/islamic_generator.py`, or trace back from an already generated target date; what matters is that the object ultimately checked is still the entry in the country calendar. If you stop at the areas around imports, grouping, or date shifting, you cannot distinguish date revisions from name revisions.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> EstimatedDate
    EstimatedDate --> ConfirmedDate: Date confirmation
    EstimatedDate --> LocalNameSelection: Check name
    ConfirmedDate --> LocalNameSelection: Check name
    LocalNameSelection --> LocalNamePreserved: Name available
    LocalNameSelection --> NormalLanguageFallback: Name unavailable
    LocalNamePreserved --> [*]
    NormalLanguageFallback --> [*]
```

The diagram does not depict "name available" as a confirmation condition. The two lines from the date states into name selection are precisely the boundary preserved by this correction: confirmation and language selection both need to be checked, but one cannot substitute for the other. Normal language fallback remains a branch of name selection, not the endpoint of the confirmation path or a failure indicator.

## Review excerpts and subsequent changes of position

One reminder from the review was: "Look for counterexamples first. If a confirmed record can still be labeled with two different statuses depending on the language selection, then this is not a naming issue." This comment did not dictate where to implement the change, but it brought the debate back to something that could be checked: the same confirmed date should not be misread as still being in the estimated stage because its local name is retained.

Another comment was more specific: do not erase language differences just to demonstrate name stability. Stability should mean that an entry under the same language selection carries no extraneous traces of migration, not that all calls must return English, nor that all languages have the same translation in every year. This comment corrected the early, sweeping claim that "it is enough for the name to remain unchanged."

Another discussion attempted to fold "unknown language" into confirmation handling: since confirming the date requires an explicit output, unknown languages should always return the default name. This proposal was not accepted. Unknown-language fallback is a normal branch of name selection; date confirmation only requires that the date and entry be finalized, and cannot thereby define a cross-language fallback policy. Combining the two would make future language fixes look like date migrations.

The review did not require extending Bangladesh's handling into a uniform rule for all Islamic holidays. The date sources, language support, and confirmation cadence for different countries are not uniformly defined by this record. The generation path includes date shifts and grouping, and there is no evidence to support consolidating every country, language, or religious source under the same migration strategy.

From this point onward, the decision on this page is narrowed to three points: confirmation status is not hidden in the display name; an available local name is not removed because of confirmation; date confirmation and language fallback are checked separately. It does not replace the rules for other countries or financial calendars, nor does it assign a unique responsibility to each internal object in the generator.

## Early Cases Retained for Background

Two examples in early drafts were treated as evidence of "general religious-holiday behavior." They are retained now only as historical background.

The first example treated any local-script text as a temporary value that had not yet been normalized, and recommended standardizing it to English after confirmation. This was precisely the third step later discarded. It overlooked that a local name may itself be the calendar's normal outward-facing representation, and did not distinguish whether a name change came from a source revision or a confirmation migration.

The second example treated the hint after the name as the sole source of status, assuming that once the hint disappeared, it could be asserted that the date was confirmed. This judgment no longer applies either. The hint may come from an old display strategy; the name itself is not a record of the date source. Investigation must go back to the entry's date and confirmation path, rather than comparing strings alone.

Neither of these old examples was carried forward into the current requirements. They are retained here because discussions of legacy calls still refer to phrases such as "standardize to English" or "hint disappeared"; when you encounter these phrases, you should know that they come from ideas that were not adopted. They are not operational instructions retained for compatibility.

Another early opinion held that, since the generator uses `defaultdict`, the language name should be fixed during aggregation. This judgment was likewise not adopted. Aggregation provides only visible local adjacency; it cannot by itself prove at which step the display name was selected. This opinion is retained so that later reviewers know why someone once followed the aggregation logic to look for name differences.

## Adjacent Issues Still Not Split Out

One adjacent issue has not yet been split out: if the source first provides a local name and an estimated date, then revises the holiday's translated name during subsequent confirmation, the caller will see changes to both the date and the name at the same time. It is not possible to determine in advance which of the two causes the user-facing difference. The current decision only prohibits proactively switching to the default language to indicate confirmation; it does not prohibit the source itself from revising the name.

Another unresolved point is historical queries. Whether results already produced by an older version should retain the estimate hint from that time, or be returned under the current naming rules when regenerated, depends on whether the particular query stores the entry as it was when generated. This page does not contain enough material to establish this as a backfill strategy. When this issue arises, first confirm whether the query retrieved a historical result or a regenerated calendar, then decide whether a separate compatibility note is needed.Regional aliases, financial calendars, or subdivision outputs still cannot be brought into this decision. Their object scopes are different. Even if religious holidays or localized names also exist somewhere, Bangladesh's confirmation handling must not be reused merely because the strings are similar. This restriction does not deny that they may have similar issues, but prevents a correction to one national calendar from inadvertently becoming a shared rule.

These issues are not included in the current decision because they respectively concern source revisions, historical results, and other calendar scopes, rather than being another expression of the same output relationship between Bangladesh's confirmed dates and Bengali names. Deciding on all of them together would burden what should be a local fix with additional interface commitments.

## Current release guidance

After the corrections above, the current requirement targets only two sample dates in the Bangladesh national calendar and handles date confirmation, name language, and estimated indicators separately: the Bangladesh national calendar labels 2024-02-26 as শবে বরাত Shab-e-Barat, and on 2026-05-28 uses ঈদুল আজহা to mark the confirmed Eid al-Adha; names for confirmed dates must not carry an estimated suffix.

This statement replaces the part of the old draft that said "return to default English after confirmation"; it does not replace the ordinary unknown-language fallback. The first date is retained as a local-name sample, and the second date is used as a sample to confirm that no estimation trace remains once confirmation is finalized; only checking both together avoids fixing only one half.

During implementation review, scope the review to the national calendar first; do not misread this as a requirement for a financial calendar or a particular subdivision. If the result date is correct but the name carries an estimated indicator, inspect where the confirmation status is applied to the entry; if the date is correct and has no indicator but the name falls back to English, inspect the branch for language selection and local-name retention. If the target language has no name to begin with, follow that language's existing fallback rules; do not interpret the absence as a confirmation failure.

This requirement applies directly only to the two specified dates. It does not require every name in the estimation phase to be exactly the same as in the confirmation phase, nor does it claim that all future holidays will be free of source revisions. What it requires is that a confirmed target date must not rely on an estimated suffix to preserve the appearance of its old state, nor lose a usable Bengali name because of the confirmation action.

## Recording after the decision

This page no longer recommends using "renaming" to describe this type of revision. When recording a change, at minimum clearly identify the object: whether it is date confirmation, a name revision, or a language fallback. All three may appear as different strings in the output, but the maintenance actions are different.

For date-confirmation changes, first record the target date and confirmation result; for a name issue, record the selected language and actual name; for a language fallback, record why the local name is unavailable. The resulting record can explain why a holiday entry changed, without forcing readers to infer internal state from the English and local text.

The wording about "keeping the name unchanged" in the old version can still serve as a reference for the intent: do not let the transition to confirmed status needlessly disrupt the display. But it can no longer be used to oppose actual name revisions provided by the source, nor can it be used to require all languages to share one name. The current decision protects the continuity of local names on confirmed dates, and the absence of an estimate suffix after confirmation.

## Appendix: Judgments that were previously conflated

- "The presence of Bengali means the date has been confirmed." Overturned. Language is the result of name selection, not evidence of confirmation.
- "English is the safest choice after confirmation." Overturned. Defaulting to English is not a way to indicate confirmed status.
- "As long as the notice is removed, the date is guaranteed to be usable." Overturned. Whether the date itself has entered the confirmation path must be checked.
- "The generator file determines all output semantics." No longer adopted. This entry point is useful for troubleshooting, but the actual relationship between names and dates should still be checked against the generated entries.

These judgments are not retained to maintain compatibility with them. They are part of this page's history, and also explain why the current requirements specify only two dates, two Bengali name variants and the confirmation suffix, rather than also cramming in all behavior for other countries, other calendar categories or unknown languages.

Current scope ruling (v2): Current scope ruling: The Bangladesh baseline has no generic Islamic generation path, and this round requires only the two dates confirmed by announcements for DOC-12, not new holidays in 2030 or a new islamic_show_estimated parameter. Preserving existing estimates for other years refers to calendars such as Indonesia whose baselines already include estimates; Indonesia's switch and the second day after confirmation still follow the existing behavior. Current scope ruling: Adding en_US translations for the new names is not mandatory; returning the source text when an entry is missing from the catalog is a valid gettext fallback, and must not be marked incorrect because it matches the local name. Preserve existing translations, the rule that explicitly supported languages take precedence over the environment, and the existing environment fallback for unknown languages.

# Indonesia Holiday Category Adjustment Proposal

The previous version treated collective leave as an add-on to public holidays, solely because callers wanted one fewer branch. On review, that isn't enough to justify merging them by default: `holidays/countries/indonesia.py` has already introduced both `GOVERNMENT` and `PUBLIC`, so categories are, at a minimum, something the file needs to express explicitly. We shouldn't start by treating one of them as a display label.

The revised proposal is to retain two layers of selection. Public holiday dates would still be queried using the public holiday category; callers that need collective leave would explicitly include GOVERNMENT. This keeps name selection and category selection from standing in for one another: the former controls the text users see, while the latter determines whether a date is included in the results.

Language handling is still undecided. The file uses `gettext as tr`, which shows that names pass through a translation entry point, but that is not enough to specify which text must be returned for an unknown language. An early proposal suggested mapping unknown languages directly to a particular local name; that suggestion lacks verifiable output samples, so we'll keep it as an earlier proposal rather than treat it as an API commitment.

What we need is not more translation tables, but two sets of actual results: one with only the public holiday category selected, and one that also includes GOVERNMENT. The date sets should be compared under the same language setting; then check separately whether switching languages changes names without changing categories. The month constant imports only show that the file is organized by Gregorian months; they should not be used to infer the source of any religious date calculations.

If splitting the categories causes existing calls to miss collective leave, the rollback should restore those calls' previous result scope rather than merge all dates back into the default set. At the time, we hadn't yet compiled a list of which existing calls depended on that scope.

# Proposal to Adjust Indonesia's Holiday Categories

This proposal has been retained because legacy calls still raise the question of why names and dates for Indonesia are separate concerns. The earliest version included collective leave in the public-holiday results and treated language as a side issue; that order now looks like too much of a shortcut, but the original paragraphs are retained to help explain why the category split was introduced later.

The old proposal assumed that callers only cared whether a given day was a day off. It did not distinguish public holidays from government collective leave, nor did it provide a separate decision point for unknown languages. That approach worked for a temporary display, but in a country calendar API it collapsed two choices into one: callers could not change only the category while keeping the naming conditions unchanged.

The later review started with the objects adjacent to `holidays/countries/indonesia.py`. That file imports `gettext as tr`, along with `GOVERNMENT` and `PUBLIC`; the month constants come from the Gregorian calendar module. This information is not enough to reconstruct the source of every holiday, but it is enough to reject the old assumption that "categories are just wording." Categories and the translation entry point already appear separately at this layer, so the proposal should also let callers choose them independently.

## Retained Original Proposal

The first draft recommended including collective leave in the default results so users would not need to understand additional constants. This rationale did not address the counterexample: some users only need public holidays, and including collective leave by default would change their date set. The first draft also recommended using local names directly for unknown languages. That was not a conclusion drawn from sample outputs, only a working assumption written down to avoid blanks in the UI.

Neither point has been removed from the historical versions. The former is no longer the direction for the API; the latter still cannot be treated as a language fallback rule. In particular, do not read "translatable" as "all languages already have language-specific names," or infer from a displayed name that the category selection is correct.

## Trial Scope After the Split

This trial is limited to the API boundary between categories and names; it is not an opportunity to revise the sources of Indonesia's dates. Public queries retain the public-holiday set; callers that need collective leave add GOVERNMENT as part of the same intended query. Language selection continues through the existing translation entry point. The actual result for unknown languages is listed separately as an item to verify, rather than specifying an unverified default name here.

The results that must be preserved are as follows: on 2026-03-21, the Indonesia country calendar uses Hari Raya Idul Fitri to mark the confirmed Eid al-Fitr; when the GOVERNMENT category is selected, 2026-02-16 should also yield Cuti Bersama Tahun Baru Imlek.

This statement imposes two distinct requirements. The first half confirms that the name for the date is not tentative; the second requires that collective leave must not disappear as a result of simplifying the public-query path. It does not mean that all Indonesia dates fall under GOVERNMENT, or that selecting GOVERNMENT replaces PUBLIC. How callers pass category combinations still needs to be checked against the current public entry point.

## Comparison Method and Rollback Point

During the trial, first hold the language conditions fixed and examine the date sets for the public-holiday selection and for the selection with GOVERNMENT added. Compare added dates only when the category changes; then examine names under the same category conditions. This avoids misreporting translation differences as date differences, or missing category selections as language fallback issues.

If a legacy call does in fact depend on collective leave being included by default, the category split cannot immediately be rolled out as the only entry point. On rollback, first restore the scope of results that call originally received, then record whether it needs a public-holiday calendar or a calendar that includes collective leave. This rollback point is based on compatibility, not a long-term commitment to all users.

Unknown languages remain an unfinished item. The available material only shows that names pass through `tr`; it does not provide an output for an unknown language that could serve as a general rule. The next addition should include actual returned content, not another speculative set of translation priorities.

DOC-14 covers the separation of India's national and subdivision scopes; its conclusions about boundaries cannot be used in place of category decisions for Indonesia. Both involve date sets, but what is being split is different.

# Market Special Date Migration Procedure

The earlier investigation paused at `holidays/financial/ny_stock_exchange.py`. At the time, the area near the top of the file showed date types, Gregorian calendar primitives, `HALF_DAY`, `PUBLIC`, and the ChristianHolidays, InternationalHolidays, and StaticHolidays groups. This gives us a place to look near the financial objects: if all that remains of an existing sample is an issue name or call name, start here to look for adjacent dates and categories. It does not establish a shared implementation for KRX, Saudi Arabia, or TSX, nor does directory proximity justify merging national holidays with exchange closures.

The first-round note listed NASDAQ, CME, KRX, Saudi Arabia, and TSX together only to avoid omissions. For each output, first retain the object, input date, original name, and category; if the same date appears twice, do not collapse the entries yet. Exchange closures, national public holidays, and observed dates that may fall on weekdays can each appear as a date result; matching dates are not enough to establish that they are the same thing.

The working assumption at the time was that special dates only supplement a static date table, and differences in names mainly affect display. There were not yet enough counterexamples to this assessment, so leave it in the record as written; it does not justify removing names or merging results for different objects on the same day. If a name changes later, retain the original string first, then determine whether the change comes from the language, the object, or the event itself.

For this migration round, first collect samples in this order:

1. Retrieve output from old calls, including the object and input date.
2. Compare exchange objects separately; do not mix them with national calendars in the same table.
3. For weekend inputs, keep a separate record of the originally scheduled date and the date actually returned.
4. Decide whether to replace the old records only after both dates and names are available for review.

If you can find only a single date line, treat it as a lead first, not as a conclusion that the exchange is closed. If the pre-call state cannot be restored, retain the output already obtained and do not change the shared groupings. The weekend sample for TSX has not yet been retrieved independently; this version also leaves the name format for Saudi Arabia undecided. If the national level and subdivisions are included in later checks, they should come with their own language or region tags; do not fill in their details from the financial samples.

# Market Special Date Migration Process

The first version was just a note that used the financial file as a starting point for checking earlier records. On review, the issue wasn't copying the dates again, but that the early records didn't say which object a result row belonged to. Exchanges, country calendars, and subdivisions can all provide dates and names, but those fields don't have the same meaning at each object level. If all results are put into one table, then when rows are missing or extra rows appear, there's no way to tell which sample batch to revisit for further checks.

The old entry point is still `holidays/financial/ny_stock_exchange.py`. The file header directly shows the following adjacent items:

```python
from datetime import date
from holidays.constants import HALF_DAY, PUBLIC
```

The same location also shows Gregorian calendar primitives and groupings such as ChristianHolidays, InternationalHolidays, and StaticHolidays. This entry point is useful for recovering date and category records previously left near the financial objects. It is not an ownership table for cross-market rules; the object boundaries for KRX, Saudi Arabia, and TSX still need to be preserved in their respective samples. File location cannot substitute for those boundaries.

## The Old Three-Column Table

The early table had only "Date, Market closed?, Notes." It was handy for an initial scan: it was easy to see whether a given day had any output. But it collapsed three independent questions into one judgment. First, which object the call input belonged to; second, whether the original name was retained; third, which category the result appeared under. The table had no exchange field and no place for the original date. Once an observed date for a weekend was entered, it looked no different from a regular workday result.

The three-column table stays. It can still indicate that a date was noticed before, but it no longer serves as the post-migration verification record. New records must retain at least the object, input date, exported name, and category. For country samples, add language or subdivision fields according to the actual differences; for weekend samples, add the original and observed dates. These fields are not meant to force all objects into the same table format, but to let whoever takes over understand why a result row belongs to that batch.

There was another early shortcut: first translate the returned name into a short Chinese label, then compare it together with the date. That practice was stopped. Short labels strip out the original language form and can make outputs from different objects on the same date look like the same record. From that point on, samples retain the original strings, with Chinese explanations alongside them rather than overwriting the returned values.

## Three Batches of Records

The exchange batch retains the object name, input date, exported name, and category. Even if two exchanges produce the same string, keep a row for each; matching names do not mean matching objects. Nor can the category be inferred from the name. A name that looks like a public holiday does not mean that the exchange's record should be interpreted as a regular public holiday.

The country batch first establishes the country level, then checks whether the subdivision has entries of its own. A country-level result cannot simply be copied to the regional level; local entries cannot be promoted to country-level results just because their dates or names are similar. In this batch, the language field is not a display add-on but part of the differences in the original names. When a name needs explanation, readers should still be able to see the actual returned string.

The weekend batch handles original dates and observed dates separately. If a call shows only one side, record only the result actually seen; do not fill in the name, category, or date for the other side. Matching workday samples cannot stand in for weekend samples; incomplete weekend results also do not permit filling in the entire batch as regular public holidays. It must be possible to look back at the relationship between the original input and the returned date. Otherwise, later checks cannot determine whether the boundary comes from the input or the result.

## Two Cleanup Attempts That Were Stopped

One cleanup attempt planned to use workday samples to explain weekend handling: if the workday samples matched, separate weekend records would no longer be kept. That approach was not pursued. Workday output cannot establish whether the original date produces an observed date, or which object a rolled-forward result belongs to. Weekend samples must start from their own inputs; they cannot be treated as a note appended to workday records.

Another cleanup attempt kept only the final output row, omitting the input date and object. That meant even if a name change was discovered later, there was no way to tell whether it was a regular holiday, a special date, or a rolled-forward result. Old records can be kept as traces of the original state, but they cannot be used to directly replace the migration results. A date without an object label can only flag a possible difference; it is not enough for maintainers to assign a record to an exchange or country batch.

The review margin note was brief: "Confirm the object first, then look at the date; don't discard names as noise." If dates match but names differ, retain both original outputs first; if names match but objects differ, do not make one an alias of the other. Another comment was that when a row is missing or there is an extra row, first check whether the input crosses a weekend, then return to old samples for the same object rather than immediately changing the public grouping.

The review also raised a question that had no answer: does the caller use names only for display, or does it go on to filter by name? No information is available at present to make that judgment on the caller's behalf. During migration, therefore, continue preserving names, do not introduce an alias layer here, and do not bundle display-format changes and date logic into a single change.

## Migrating Off the Old Calls

Migration does not overwrite old outputs with current outputs. First collect object-level samples from the old calls, then run the same inputs through the current entry point, and finally compare by object. Old records are the comparison baseline; they do not automatically establish that the current result is wrong.

When a date row is missing or there is an extra date row, first confirm the input range and where the weekend falls, then find old samples for the same object. If the date matches but the name differs, retain the original text and confirm the object and language before making a judgment; if workday results match but weekend results differ, separate the original date from the observed date. Old records without object labels can only flag a possible difference; they cannot directly trigger replacement.

If the state before the call cannot be reproduced, stop the batch and retain the old and new outputs along with the fields where they differ. Do not hide date differences by changing names, or object differences by changing categories. Cross-language display forms for Saudi Arabia remain undecided; the weekend boundary for TSX still needs further checking with independent samples.
