This page contains several generations of records: the earliest was a sheet of paper beside the finance directory, followed by on-call notes in the margins, an explanation of a failed attempt to organize the material into a table, a unified approach crossed out during review, and the object-level results that the current version needs to retain. These rules were not all formed at the same time. The old passages remain here to explain why certain fields could no longer be omitted later; the current migration still reconstructs samples by object and input, rather than collapsing all market dates into a single set of conventions.

The earliest surviving entry point is `holidays/financial/ny_stock_exchange.py`. Earlier investigations led here through issue names and call names. Near the top of the file, you can see `date`, Gregorian calendar primitives, `HALF_DAY`, `PUBLIC`, and groupings such as ChristianHolidays, InternationalHolidays, and StaticHolidays. This location can lead readers back to existing code and old records near the financial objects; it is not evidence that NASDAQ, CME, KRX, Saudi Arabia, and TSX all belong to the same group. Later, someone read "start by opening this" as "all related rules are determined here", which is one of the reasons for retaining the early notes.

## Summer 2023: A Sheet of Paper to Catch Omissions

The initial version put NASDAQ, CME, KRX, Saudi Arabia, and TSX on the same line. That line was only a first-pass check for omissions, not a compatibility matrix. At the time, the first step was to check whether anything was returned for a given date, then write dates that looked similar together; object names, input dates, names, and categories were not consistently separated. When two rows of results appeared for the same day, they were often casually merged into one. Weekday samples were also once used to guess weekend behavior.

The original note contained a working hypothesis, retained here with its original meaning: special dates are probably just a supplement to the static date table, and differences in names should not affect callers. That judgment was later narrowed in scope and can no longer be treated as a requirement for the current migration. It remains here because it led to two later misjudgments: one treated names as display text that could be discarded, and the other treated observed dates as results that could be directly adjusted away based on the input date.

The only explicit action at the time was to retain dated samples from the old calls, then check the new entry point using the same dates. Looking back now, this action left out the object field. Samples without object names can indicate that "a result was once returned for a certain day", but cannot establish whether it belonged to an exchange closure, a national public holiday, or another holiday grouping. The old samples were not removed, but are no longer used as object-level findings.

An early note also suggested "put Saturday and Sunday last." The original intent was for the initial scan to go through all weekdays first; it was later misread as saying that weekends could be left unchecked. This marginal note is retained here and marked as no longer applicable. The current migration must not use it as a reason to skip weekend inputs, and in particular must not replace observed-date records with a weekday's output.

That version did not treat language as a field that needed to be preserved. Names were regarded merely as human-readable text and were changed to short labels when convenient. Later discrepancies at the boundaries showed that short labels made it impossible to distinguish between the original language, different objects, and special events. Therefore, the early shorthand is retained only as a historical trace and is no longer used to compare old and new results.

## Additional Notes in the Margins of the On-Call Sheet

The later on-call addendum was only a few lines long: "When there are two results for the same day, do not collapse them yet." Financial objects need to retain the exchange name and closure category; country objects need to retain the country, subdivision, or language; weekend dates go in a separate place. This addendum did not establish a table of fields that all calendars should share; it only changed the habit of "merging whenever the dates are the same."

Name handling was also changed once at that time. Early records would first translate the returned names into short Chinese labels, then use those labels to compare old and new results. The short labels looked tidy, but did not reveal whether differences came from the original language, different objects, or the special events themselves. From then on, migration samples prioritized retaining the original returned values; Chinese explanations could only be written alongside them and could not replace the strings.

On-call work established a practical stopping point: do not continue interpreting output that lacks object labels, and first recover the samples from before the call; if no old output for the same input can be found, do not retroactively record the current output as "passed" either. This stopping point does not mean that all differences are equally serious, but exists because the date itself cannot distinguish ordinary holidays, special closures, and observed dates. When the object and input are missing, the next maintainer has no way to determine which batch of records to return to for review.

The addendum also included an easily overlooked restriction: if only the final output remains, do not fill in old rows using names or categories obtained later. Rows filled in this way look complete, but actually splice together information obtained at different times. Old rows can still indicate that an anomaly once occurred, but can no longer serve to restore the baseline.

That on-call shift left an unresolved question: do callers treat names only as display fields, or will they continue filtering by name? The existing material has no answer. This page has therefore continued to preserve names, does not establish an alias layer during migration, and does not bundle display-format changes and date determination into the same change. This question is still retained below because it affects whether the display layer can be standardized separately, but does not affect what should be preserved during migration.

## Autumn 2023: Batches Are No Longer Organized by File

The second round of organization no longer proceeded file by file through the directories, but instead split the records along object boundaries. The reason for splitting them was not to add table columns, but that each batch needed to retain different context. The financial file entry point is still useful, but a single path cannot be used to determine where all three object types belong.

The minimum fields recorded for an exchange batch are the object name, input date, exported name, and category. When two exchanges return the same string, keep a separate row for each. Identical names do not mean identical objects, and the category cannot be inferred from the name either. A name that looks like a public holiday does not mean it should be treated as an ordinary public holiday in the exchange records.

For country batches, check the country level first, then check whether subdivision has separate entries. A country-level result cannot simply be copied to the regional level; nor can local entries be promoted to country-level results just because their names or dates are similar. The language field serves a practical purpose in this batch: it records the form of the name actually returned by the object, rather than being a decorative column added to the financial samples.

Weekend batches separate the original date from the observed date. When a call returns only one side, save only what was actually returned, without fabricating a name, category, or date for the other side. Passing weekday results cannot substitute for weekend samples; nor can weekend results that are still incomplete, in turn, justify recording the entire batch as ordinary public holidays.

The split here does not require every batch to have the same number of fields. When exchange samples lack an object or category, object-level comparison cannot be completed; when country samples lack language or subdivision, it may be impossible to explain name differences; when weekend records lack the original date, it is impossible to determine whether the results came from observance handling. The purpose of the fields is to preserve boundaries, not to produce a pretty consolidated table.

At the time, the role of `holidays/financial/ny_stock_exchange.py` was narrowed to an entry point for looking things up. The context around the file can help locate the existing date types, categories, and holiday groupings for financial objects, but it cannot establish that the rules for KRX, Saudi Arabia, and TSX are all determined in the same place. For differences across objects, first return to the samples and object labels, rather than inferring the full implementation chain from the path location.

## Why that three-column table was not deleted

Initially, there was a three-column table with "Date, Whether the market is closed, Notes". It was well suited to visual scanning: at a glance, you could see whether a result appeared for a given day. But it compressed three different judgments into one—whether the date was correct, whether the name was preserved, and whether the object was categorized correctly. Without the exchange field, readers could not trace back to the specific object; without the original date, observed dates could not be distinguished from market closures on ordinary weekdays either.

The three-column table was retained as the earliest indication of anomalies, and was no longer used as a reference for post-migration checks. The minimum record added later contained four items: object, input date, exported name, and category. These "four items" do not require country, exchange, and weekend records to all take the form of the same table: country samples can add language or subdivision as needed, and weekend samples can add the original date and observed date as needed.

Someone once proposed standardizing on "Date, Name, Brief notes" as the three columns, on the grounds that this would be faster to read. That approach was not pursued. Country samples would lose their language and regional hierarchy, the categories in exchange samples would become notes that could not be compared, and weekend samples would again lose the original date. Making the table tidy did not reduce migration costs, but instead left each row with less of the context needed to trace back to the old call.

Another old suggestion was: save complete records only for objects with different names, and keep only dates for the remaining objects. That was not adopted either. Names matching for now does not mean that categories, objects, or weekend placement also match; if fields are only added after differences appear, the old samples can no longer be aligned with the new ones. Migration must start from the object and input, not from results that "look different".

The "Whether the market is closed" column in the three-column table also makes it easy to turn differences between objects into a binary judgment. It can indicate that the person recording it saw some kind of result at the time, but it cannot explain whether this was an exchange closure, a public holiday, or a date after the observed day. When retaining this table, treat it as the place where differences were first discovered, rather than as the final explanation of categories.

## Two explanations that did not work out

One review recorded "no name returned" as "no market closure date." On further review of the existing output, these two observations cannot be treated as interchangeable: date results and name results need to be recorded separately. This correction only changes how the results are recorded, does not establish how callers use names, and does not show that all cases with no name fall under the same rule.

Another review treated rolling dates forward from weekends as a correction to the input date, and planned to have the rolled-forward date overwrite the original date. That approach was stopped. For an observed date, at least the object, the originally scheduled date, and the rolled-forward date should be visible together; if any one is missing, only a discrepancy can be recorded, and the weekend rule cannot be declared confirmed. If the rolled-forward date overwrites the original date, later readers will be unable to tell whether the boundary came from the call input or the returned result.

Both misjudgments left the same gap: only the last line of output was saved. The last line might come from a special event, or it might be the result of observed-date processing. Without the input and the object, whoever takes over cannot tell whether to recover samples from the exchange, country, or weekend batch.

There was also a more modest attempt: comparing only "whether there is a date," without comparing names and categories. It looked like it could shorten the first round of checks, but it would collapse language differences, special closure names, and ordinary holiday names into a single Boolean judgment. The three-column table had already shown the consequences of this compression, so no separate migration checklist was created to record only whether there was a result.

Someone had also considered backfilling the object field after a discrepancy appeared. This did not become a formal step either. When backfilling the field, the person recording the results would be looking at final output already detached from the call context, and could not confirm whether the object really corresponded to that day. The object must be saved along with the input, rather than filled in from memory after the name looks unusual.

## Two remarks in the review margins

The first remark left during the review was: "Confirm the object first, then look at the date; names must not be discarded as noise." It changed the order of checks, and did not specify concrete dates for any region. If the dates are the same but the names differ, first save both sets of raw output; if the names are the same but the objects differ, do not treat either entry as an alias for the other.

The second remark was: when you see only one date discrepancy, do not immediately change the public grouping, first determine whether it is a special event or an observed date. This reminder explains why the early steps were not deleted in their entirety. The early steps can still help detect anomalies, but cannot directly determine which category an anomaly should fall into, nor can they justify changing public categories.

The review also required "seeing a result on a working day" and "the weekend boundary has been confirmed" to be written separately. The former only indicates that a particular input produces output; the latter also requires that the originally scheduled date and the observed date can both be reviewed together. This requirement was later incorporated into how the weekend batch was recorded, but was not expanded into a description of a unified algorithm for all calendars.

Someone said in the meeting: "List all the markets first, then get a successful run through them before breaking them down further." This remark is still useful for the initial scan and can help avoid missing objects; it is no longer suitable for wrapping up. A market list cannot replace object-level comparisons, nor can one successful call be recorded as completion of the entire batch.

Another old remark was: "Seeing a result on Monday is enough, look at weekends separately." It explains why the early records lacked observed dates, but it is no longer the current procedure. Weekend samples still need to be retrieved separately; the name, original date, and rolled-forward date should be matchable to one another, and if any one is missing, only a discrepancy should be recorded.

A marginal note was also retained in the review: a category must not be filled in prematurely just because a name "looks like a public holiday." This reminder was not expanded into a complete classification rule, and only required that the migration records faithfully preserve the object's category at the time. Before changing a category, complete the object-level comparison; do not replace the original marker just to make the old and new tables look consistent.

## The abandoned unified approach

An earlier proposal that had not been split up recommended putting special dates for all exchanges into the same set of static rules, exporting them uniformly under a public category, and leaving weekend dates to the calling layer. Its advantages were fewer entry points and apparent readability; the cost was that object names, market-closure semantics, and observed dates would be reinterpreted at different layers. Exchange boundaries would disappear within the unified category, and weekend samples would also lose comparable records kept in a single place.

That proposal is now marked as abandoned. It is retained not as a continued recommendation, but to explain why the public category was not simply treated as the common answer for all objects during migration. If you start your investigation with the old records, after reading this section you should continue to the object-level recovery actions below, rather than fill in missing rows based on a unified static table.

Another variant advocated replacing the original names with internal short names, then using those short names to drive comparisons. This variant was not adopted either. Short names can help readability, but they cannot prove that two returned strings are the same in language, object, or event. In particular, when exchange objects and country objects appear together, merging them by short name first would hide differences that should be preserved.

Another approach that was not pursued was to correct weekend dates only in the calling layer, without retaining the originally scheduled dates in the sample table. This approach cannot be used either. It would hide whether a change occurred between the call input and the returned date; even if a Monday result row were found later, there would be no way to tell whether it was an ordinary weekday record, an observed date, or the result of the calling layer changing the input.

## What is actually retained during migration

When migrating from legacy calls to the current entry point, do not overwrite the old output with the current output. First obtain object-level legacy samples, with each sample including both the object and the input date; then query the current entry point with the same set of inputs; finally, compare the results by object. The legacy path provides a comparison baseline, not automatic proof that the current rules are wrong, and it does not permit combining different objects into a single conclusion.

When one date row is missing or one extra row appears, first check whether the input spans a weekend, then find legacy samples for the same object. Do not change names first, and do not change the public grouping first. If a legacy sample has only a date and no object, set it aside for investigation first; it can indicate a difference, but cannot directly drive a rollback.

When dates match but names differ, retain the original text, confirm the object and language, and only then determine whether the difference is an expected change. The original text is retained here not to maintain a translation table on this page, but to prevent internal short names from prematurely merging different strings. If output in different languages is rewritten first, subsequent comparisons are left with only explanatory text, and the actual returned values are lost.

When weekday results match but weekend results differ, separate the original date from the observed date. You cannot use passing weekday results in place of the weekend batch, nor can you conclude that the original date has been corrected just because a weekend row appears. Observed-date records state only the actual input and the actual return value; when the available material is insufficient, stop at the boundary differences rather than extrapolate them into a general weekend algorithm.

When the pre-call state cannot be reproduced, stop the current batch and do not delete the old output. You may undo the overwrite from the current batch, then make a legacy call with the same date; if the legacy call cannot be reproduced either, retain both the old and new outputs and mark the fields that differ. Changing names to make dates appear consistent, or changing categories to make objects appear consistent, will both cause the next round of review to lose the original clues.

```text
Legacy call samples
  Object + input date + original output
             |
             v
Query the current entry point with the same set of inputs
             |
             v
Compare by object
  |-- Dates differ: first check the weekend placement, then look for legacy samples
  |-- Names differ: retain the original text, check the object and language
  `-- Weekends differ: keep the originally scheduled date and the observed date separate
             |
             v
Unable to confirm: retain the difference, do not overwrite legacy samples
```

The branches in the diagram describe only the sequence for restoring object-level samples. They do not combine financial objects, country objects, and subdivision objects under a single rule, nor do they decide display names for callers. If a rollback is needed, roll back a single override for the current object, without overwriting the entire batch; an unconfirmed weekend difference should not rewrite existing records for other objects.

When restoring the old path, compare the same object with the same inputs, rather than looking for a date that appears similar. If historical samples show only dates, first keep them separate from object-level samples. They are still worth keeping: they can indicate that a difference occurred previously; but they lack the context needed to overwrite current records.

## Boundary counterexamples provided by country objects

Although this comparison started at the financial entry point, the country and subdivision samples show why dates alone are not enough. Bangladesh's local names should be preserved as they are; Indonesia's confirmation status and the GOVERNMENT category need to be kept separate; India's national calendar and subdivision cannot be replaced by a single country-level sample either. These objects are not implemented as extensions of the financial module, they simply make it clear that "a date is returned" does not mean the object boundaries are correct.

The Bangladesh case reminds those recording the data that the language form must not be erased by convenient internal translated names. Even if the date has been confirmed, the name is still part of the returned content. Once local strings have been converted into standardized short names, subsequent maintainers cannot tell from the migration table whether the change occurred in date confirmation, language selection, or display-layer transliteration.

The Indonesia case is different. Here, the confirmation status and the GOVERNMENT category need to be considered separately. Similar names or similar dates do not indicate that they belong to the same category; applying judgments from country samples to financial objects, or conversely using an exchange's category to fill in country records, will erase object boundaries in either case.

India's national entries and subdivision also provide counterexamples. Results at the national level do not mean the regional level should inherit them; entries at the regional level cannot be written back to the national level merely because their names are similar. This shows why an "object" is not just a market name, but also includes the calendar hierarchy. For results of this kind, if subdivision information is missing, stop at the country batch, rather than filling in a seemingly reasonable answer from another batch.

When country samples get mixed into a financial batch, first return to the object markers, without changing the financial module's public grouping. The reverse is also true: exchange closure samples cannot be used to explain the confirmation status of a country calendar, and there is no reason for country-level names or categories to migrate automatically to exchange objects.

This page does not expand the national calendars into a complete migration workflow. They remain here because these counterexamples explain why the three batches of records cannot fill in for one another. National samples that still require verification continue to be maintained as their own objects rather than being merged into the financial result tables for convenience.

## Current verification order

The current review starts with the object, date, original name, category, and boundaries. For financial objects, first return to the area around the existing financial module, then use the same input to check weekdays and weekends separately; national calendars are handled as a separate group, and subdivision results are not merged back into the national level. When a migration can proceed, it must at least be possible to answer: Who does this row belong to, what is the input date, what name is actually returned, what is the category, and does it involve a weekend observation?

Before formally writing to the current records, first check whether the old samples have object labels. Old rows without labels are not discarded, but they cannot directly replace the current object-level results. If the input range crosses a weekend, establish the weekend batch first; if it does not cross a weekend, still do not delete the name and category merely because the date matches. The sequence may seem slower than the old three-column list, but in practice it reduces the number of times later that the meaning of old rows must be guessed.

NASDAQ and CME both use National Day of Mourning for former President Jimmy Carter to mark the market as closed on 2025-01-09, KRX uses 신정연휴 to mark the New Year's market closure on 2024-01-01, and Saudi Arabia uses عطلة رسمية بمناسبة عودة الملك عبد الله to mark a public holiday on 2011-02-26.

This record establishes the dates and original names of four object-level samples; it does not combine them into a single "special-date rule." Even if the two exchanges return the same name, they are still different objects; the Korean and Arabic strings must not be changed to internal labels before comparison. The current confirmation concerns the recorded results; it does not decide the format for the presentation layer.

A category cannot be inferred from the name alone. Financial market closures, public holidays, and observed days may all appear as a date and a name, but the records still need to preserve object boundaries. If a later sample fills in only a date, without an object or category, it can be included in material pending comparison, but it cannot replace the object-level output that has already been saved.

These four samples also do not constitute a template for all special dates. They show that the current records should retain the object, date, and original name together; they do not authorize backfilling the dates, names, or categories of other markets in the same way. Each new object must still enter the corresponding batch with its own input and returned result.

## Weekend tab for TSX

Keep TSX as a separate batch. First enter the originally scheduled date, then check whether a deferred date appears; the object labels in the two queries must match. Keep the name returned for 2026-12-28 as `Boxing Day`, as a record of an observed market closure resulting from a weekend deferral. It must not be recorded as a duplicate row of a normal business-day result, and the original date and observed date must be visible separately.

The old approach kept only the deferred date and deleted the holiday itself. This approach no longer applies, because readers cannot tell whether a date is the original holiday, an observed date, or input rewritten by the calling layer. When a name appears on only one side, save only the result you see, without filling in the other side.

Successful and failed calls should be kept side by side. When a call fails, first confirm whether the input still refers to the same object and the same date range; if there is no comparable old sample, stop at recording the differences. Do not backfill the entire financial batch with the public holiday category just because the weekend results are not yet complete.

TSX also shows the granularity of recovery actions: the rollback applies to a single output for the current object, not the entire financial batch. Existing records for other exchanges should not be reclassified because one weekend boundary has not yet been confirmed. If any of the original input, object, or point of failure is missing, keep only a pending-investigation flag.

The easiest mistake to make in weekend batches is to first see the business day after deferral and then write it back as a normal result for the originally scheduled date. This is not how the current records are handled. The originally scheduled date, observed date, and returned name are each kept where they can be reviewed; if the call provides only part of this information, retain that part as returned, without guessing values to fill in the remaining fields.

## Two items left for later

Whether Saudi Arabia's public holiday names need standardized formatting in the cross-language presentation layer has not been decided on this page. Name verification can continue, but do not bundle presentation-layer changes with the migration. Samples for Bangladesh, Indonesia, and India should also continue to be maintained in their respective object batches, and they must not be merged into the financial module's migration results just because they can clarify the boundaries.

Failed calls for TSX still need to retain the original input, object, and point of failure; if only the deferred date remains later, retrieve the old sample before making a judgment. If a country sample has only a name and no category, keep it for now as well, and do not fill in its category using one from the financial batch.

One related question has not yet been split off: whether callers use names for filtering. The current migration does not need to wait for an answer, because the original names have already been saved; but if the presentation side later proposes standardizing short names, that change must be handled separately from date and category comparisons. Otherwise, it will recreate the confusion left by the earlier three-column table.

## Outdated appendix

**Old example: Standardize the public holiday category.** Early samples recorded all special exchange dates as public holidays and compared only dates during migration. This example has been deprecated and is kept for historical comparison. Current records capture the exchange object, original name, and market-closure semantics, without using the public holiday category to override differences between objects.

**Old example: Keep only the deferred date.** Early weekend checks deleted the holiday itself and kept only the next business day. This example no longer applies. Currently, at least the original date and observed date are saved; when a name appears on only one side, do not fabricate it on the other side.

**Legacy example: Inferring the full implementation from the file location.** Earlier investigations treated paths as an ownership map. A path can only help locate `holidays/financial/ny_stock_exchange.py` and its neighbors, not replace object-level checks. This legacy example is retained because those taking over still often start looking for samples from the same entry point.

**Legacy example: Replacing the comparison process with the final output.** Records of this kind retain only the date or name on the final line, omitting the object and input. They can be kept as a record of what was found at the time, but can no longer serve as a basis for recovery. The current practice is to first restore object-level samples, then determine which field differs.

**Legacy example: Using weekday samples to cover weekends.** This early shortcut recorded matching weekday results as if the entire object had been checked. It is no longer applicable. Weekday results only show that the input in that run returned a result; when weekends are involved, the originally scheduled date and the observed date must still be recorded separately.

# BMV and TSX Market-Closure Boundary Trial Run Record

At first, BMV and TSX were placed in the same year-end boundary experiment. The question at hand was: when querying by date, can the exchange name be retained from the financial calendar entry point; if the base date object is changed as well, will Gregorian and Julian Basic Compatibility change the query result? This grouping is only being used to screen samples; no run results support it yet.

At the time, it was opened from `holidays/financial/shanghai_stock_exchange.py`. The file path does not match the name of this object, so the note records it only as the starting point for the investigation. At this point, what can be retained is the file location—not the implementation ownership of BMV or TSX. First inspect the declarations and adjacent objects around financial, exchanges, and day; do not put the name source, date calculation, and weekend handling on the same line.

The old assessment was: as long as the exchange file can retain a market-closure name, the two samples can be explained using the same year-end boundary. This is only a working hypothesis at this point. It does not distinguish an ordinary market-closure date from an observation date after a weekend, nor does it state whether the returned date is the exchange's original date or a deferred date.

At the next review, keep the same date query fixed and change only the exchange object. Record three things each time: the returned date, the returned name, and whether the result is an observation date. In the second round, change only Gregorian and Julian Basic Compatibility's input so the two conditions do not change at the same time. If the name is retained but the date boundary differs, the old wording, "shared year-end boundary," can no longer be used. Run output, failure nodes, and the specific call entry point have not yet been added.

This page started as an experiment worksheet comparing the two exchanges side by side. I started looking for the entry point at `holidays/financial/shanghai_stock_exchange.py`, then realized that the file location only shows that the investigation began in the financial directory; it isn't enough to attribute the implementation to BMV or TSX. The old notes are still here because they explain why closure dates and observance dates for weekend holidays were initially put in the same group.

On review, I split each query into four fields: "input date, returned name, returned date, boundary type." The aim wasn't to build a complete table: the May records only noted whether a name appeared, without recording the rationale for the date associated with it. Review regular closures, weekend shifts, and base-calendar compatibility separately; if any field is missing, don't write up the result as confirmation that the boundary has taken effect.

I've kept the old assumption here too: both exchanges could be queried through the existing entry point, so at the time I tentatively thought they could share a year-end boundary. That assumption was later narrowed. Finding a name only shows that it appeared in the query results; it doesn't show that the Monday after the weekend had already been treated as an observance date, nor that Gregorian and Julian Basic Compatibility played no part in the result. CAL-205 later required confirmation in an actual CI run, rather than treating the presence of a configuration file as a substitute for run results. That run's ID wasn't saved on this page.

The release scope retained after review is: the release for BMV on 2026-11-02 covers the Día de Muertos closure, and TSX, with Boxing Day falling on a weekend, provides a Monday observed closure on 2026-12-28; each exchange continues to be imported from the existing public financial namespace.

These two must no longer be grouped into a single "year-end sample." For the BMV field, check whether the closure name and date are returned together; for the TSX field, check the result shifted to Monday, not just whether the name appears on the weekend date. When copying names, retain the original text; in particular, don't replace accented characters with plain letters. At the CAL-220 entry point, handle Gregorian and Julian Basic Compatibility separately: reproduce it starting from the pre-call state, first record the changes left by the date query, then determine whether it is related to the exchange samples. Base compatibility behavior has not been generalized into exchange rules here.

We still need one verifiable output under the same conditions. Next time, from the same CI run, add only the BMV and TSX return values, and put regular closures and observance dates in separate columns; don't change the query entry point or swap out the test dates along the way.

# Gregorian September Fifth-Week Troubleshooting Tree

This procedure was left over from the old failed call involving "Gregorian September Fifth-Week Start". The entry point is still `tests/calendars/test_gregorian.py`. The initial record did not retain the call text, nor did it retain whether the user saw an exception, an empty result, or a date mismatch; the later review did not fill in either of these gaps. As a result, some branches below look like normal troubleshooting steps but are actually just old signposts set up at the time to keep the discussion going.

Card CAL-208 later moved to In Progress. What can be confirmed is that the investigation always concerned the start of Gregorian's fifth week of September, not holiday data for other calendars. Do not replace "September" with an arbitrary month and apply the same assessment; this entry point only addresses the boundary reported at the time.

## First, Preserve the Assessment from That Time

The old assessment is recorded here and has not been deleted: as long as the fifth occurrence of the same weekday can be found in September using the week index within the month, the start should be accepted; if the calculated week span extends into October, it can still be counted as September's fifth week. This was once treated as the default explanation.

The problem with it is not that a contradictory result already exists, but that the records never retained the original call or return value at all. Without the input, it is impossible to tell whether "the fifth week" refers to a start within the month, a particular Sunday, or an index supplied by the caller. Yet the old procedure conflated these possibilities and assumed a within-month index from the outset. That assumption is still retained so that readers of the old discussion can understand why it went in the wrong direction at the time.

At the time, "not immediately finding a corresponding test" was also treated as a sign that "the test entry point does not cover it". This branch is also retained below, but it must not be read as meaning that the behavior does not exist; it only means that the call was not reconstructed during that inspection.

## Sequence After Opening the File

At the top of the file, three types of direct clues are visible: `from datetime import date`, `from unittest import TestCase`, and the import block that imports the Gregorian object from `holidays.calendars.gregorian`. The old investigation did not require tracing the entire calendar library first, nor did it require working backward from national or financial calendar cases.

First, do two narrowly scoped things in that test file:

1. Find uses of `date` and note whether any September dates are constructed directly.
2. Find where the Gregorian object is created and where assertions are made about it, and compare the date inputs with what the assertions focus on: membership, names, or the dates themselves.

These two actions cannot be swapped. If you read the assertion text before looking at the date input, it is easy to misread an input spanning months as a result within September; if you look only at date construction and not at the assertions, you will not know whether the failure occurs when the calendar object returns its result.

The old record only says that both the issue name and the call name point here. It provides no class name, method name, command, or stack information. Do not invent these missing items as you read, and do not interpret the presence of `TestCase` as meaning that a corresponding regression sample already exists. It only shows that this file is on the test side; it cannot stand in for the specific call.

```text
Received a "start of the fifth week of September" report
|
+-- Is the original call still available?
|   |
|   +-- Yes
|   |   +-- Preserve the full form of the date argument
|   |   +-- Preserve the returned content or exception text
|   |   +-- Search the test file for the same date and the same object
|   |   `-- Both found: compare the input, assertions, and actual return value
|   |
|   `-- No
|       +-- Only a September date found: record it as a candidate sample, not as the original call
|       +-- Only a Gregorian assertion found: record it as a candidate assertion, not as the failure point
|       `-- Neither found: retain "call not reconstructed", stop attributing a cause
|
`-- Once the original call has been reconstructed, what is the result?
    |
    +-- Fails during date creation: first check whether the input falls within the reported September boundary
    +-- Calendar object returns an empty result: check whether the assertion was intended to test membership
    +-- Returned date does not match: check which date the assertion compares
    `-- Has a name but the date does not match: do not switch to guessing based on the name
```

"Returns an empty result" and "Has a name but the date does not match" in the tree are branch labels, not statements of fact about CAL-208. The original record did not save the result type, so it must be identified first during troubleshooting; do not fill in the incident narrative just because a particular branch is more familiar.

## Month-Boundary Handling in the Old Path

The old procedure required treating the last week of September as a complete candidate span first, then checking whether it crossed the end of the month. If it did not, accept it directly; if it did, still count the span as part of September. This passage was the explanation most readily quoted over and over at the time.

```
Candidate week span is within September
  -> Old procedure: accept as the start of the fifth week

Candidate week span extends from September into October
  -> Old procedure: still assign it to September, continue looking for the start

Cannot confirm where the candidate week span begins
  -> Old procedure: supply an explanation based on the within-month index
```

The final line is especially unreliable. It treats "unconfirmed" as a premise that allows calculation to continue, so even if a seemingly plausible date is obtained later, that does not show that the original report has been explained. It is retained because the early troubleshooting records really did continue along this path, not because it has been verified.

At the time, the recommendation to look at the `date` input first was intended to separate month assignment from the natural-language issue name. Whether a date object specifies September can be checked directly; exactly which week boundaries are used for "the start of the fifth week" must be determined from both the call and the assertions. The old document later collapsed these two levels of assessment into one step, leading to the misreading that "the month is known, so the week boundaries are known".

## Branches When a Test Snippet Is Found

If a test snippet directly constructs a September date, first note whether that date is an input. Do not treat a September `date` as the expected value just because you see it; it may only be part of the setup, or it may be the target of an assertion. Then check how the Gregorian object is queried around this date.

If an assertion only shows that the object contains a certain date, the old procedure treated it as supporting evidence that the start was correct. That inference is too strong: membership and the definition of the start are not the same thing. Only if the assertion compares date values should you go on to check whether that value comes from the input, the return value, or a separate construction in the test itself.

If you can find the date input but no nearby operations on the Gregorian object, record "date sample visible, call relationship not seen". Do not infer that a test was omitted, and certainly do not rewrite the old assessment on that basis.

If you can find the Gregorian object and assertions but no September date, record "object assertion visible, month sample not seen". This might be regression material for another month, or a different check in the same file; without the original call, neither possibility can be ruled out.

Only when the input, object operations, and assertions can all be placed in the same snippet is it permissible to discuss how to interpret the fifth week. The old procedure put this requirement last, leading many readers to discuss month boundaries first and then go back to look for the material. Here the order is reversed, but the old conclusions are not scrubbed away.

## Old Recovery Actions and Stopping Points

The original procedure's recovery action was: if a corresponding item could not be found quickly, continue recording it as "missing test entry point" and wait for the call to be added back. This was not a fix, and it produced no verifiable result. The later review could still confirm only the entry-point file and the visible imports; it cannot be upgraded to recovered status.

Therefore, the only stopping points still in use are these:

- No original call: do not determine whether the failure occurred in date construction, calendar return, or assertion comparison.
- No result seen by the user: do not classify the issue as an empty result, an exception, or a wrong date.
- No local snippet containing the date, Gregorian object, and assertions together: do not write a new explanation for the fifth week.
- Only the old assessment is available: it can be retained as a historical interpretation, but it cannot be used to close the card.

The old version described the third case as "handle it using the within-month index first". That note is still present, but now it is only used to identify the reasoning path in the old record. Actual troubleshooting should stop where the call is missing, rather than substitute month-boundary assumptions for evidence.

## Record Format for Review

Do not write a long narrative during review; just fill in the following rows. Blank entries should remain blank, and in particular, do not guess the date from the issue name.

| Content to retain | Known status |
| --- | --- |
| Original call syntax | Not added back |
| Input date | Not added back |
| Result seen by the user | Not added back |
| Associated test entry point | `tests/calendars/test_gregorian.py` |

This table is not a chain of proof; it only separates gaps from objects that have been seen. The problem with the old record is that it put both in the same sentence: saying that the call failed while also jumping straight into discussing week spans across months. Separating them at least prevents unknown failure behavior from being mixed into the test entry point that is already visible.

## Boundaries with Adjacent Issues

DOC-20 records another item concerning Gregorian August Last-Week Start. It can serve as an adjacent navigation item, but it cannot be used to fill in the missing call in the September report. Whether a month boundary is crossed at the end of August, which date input is used, and what result is seen do not automatically apply to the fifth week of September.

Likewise, do not look for explanations in holidays, language names, or market-closure samples from other calendars. These are not the same kind of object as week boundaries within Gregorian months. The only things to focus on here are: what date the original call supplied, how `date` appears in the test, and what the assertions on the Gregorian object actually check.

## Archival Note

This procedure still retains the old interpretations of "still assign it to September even if it crosses months" and "if no test is found, continue using the within-month index". They make the old discussion understandable, but should not be treated as new implementation instructions. After the card moved from To Do to In Progress at the time, the original call and result were not added to this material; the final troubleshooting conclusion therefore still stops at entry point located, failure behavior not reconstructed.

If the actual call becomes available later, first use it to fill in the three entries above, then start from the first level of the tree. Do not simply append a date to the old assessment to make the document look as if regression verification has been completed.

# Gregorian Reverse Fifth Week Decision Record

Treat the reverse fifth week as a standalone issue first; do not draw a conclusion directly from the adjacent reverse fourth week. The distinction to make now is whether a fifth-week request counted backward from month-end should retain its own decision trail; this is not simply a different way of writing the forward week number.

Three approaches were compared initially. First, carry forward the fourth-week result and treat the fifth week as the same type of input; second, exclude the fifth week up front to avoid inconsistencies in later records; third, retain the fifth-week request and separately record calls that produce a date and calls that cannot be reproduced reliably.

Adopt the third approach. The fourth week may serve as a nearby reference, but it must not stand in for the fifth-week result. If the two are combined from the start, then even if a date discrepancy is found later, it will be impossible to determine whether the reverse week number was rewritten or the fifth week itself was not handled independently.

This decision only requires the regression materials to retain the results from both sides. A successful call cannot substitute for a failed call; a failed call cannot be brushed aside with a single "boundary issue." What form the failure will ultimately take has not yet been determined, so it is not being written as a fixed exception convention yet.

To be added: which common inputs should be retained for each of the fifth-week request and the adjacent fourth-week request; when reliable reproduction is not possible, how granular the test record needs to be.

versions.body:
# Gregorian Reverse Fifth-Week Decision Record

The initial draft recorded the issue as "whether the fifth week is valid," but at the time it did not unpack that phrase. It was easy to treat the fifth week as a natural extension of the fourth week: since we could already count backward from month-end to the fourth week, the fifth week seemed to require only one more identical calculation. Later review did not accept that extrapolation. What needs to be preserved long term is not a generic yes or no, but the fact that the fifth-week request remains identifiable across successful and failed calls.

This record has dealt only with Gregorian month-week semantics from the outset. It does not define rules for national holidays, financial calendars, or other uses of date objects. Nor does it interpret "fifth week" as any arbitrary fifth date concept. The object here is always the fifth-week request made when counting backward from month-end, along with the result that request leaves in the test material.

The initial draft made two tradeoffs that still stand. First, the reverse-counted ordinal itself should be preserved; it must not be rewritten as an adjacent ordinal just to make the sample look tidy. Second, validity cannot be established by successful samples alone. If the record retains only a call that can produce a date, future maintainers will see only that some example once worked; if it retains only a call that cannot be reproduced reliably, it will also erase any successful case that may exist.

At the time, the following handling options were on the table. They are not a complete enumeration of implementation approaches, but a comparison of what the regression material should retain:

|Handling|What it saved at the time|Problem left behind|
|---|---|---|
|Extend from the reverse-counted fourth week to the fifth week|Write one fewer set of inputs|It becomes impossible to tell whether the fifth week was rewritten|
|Keep only successful calls|Results are easy to read|The boundary between valid and invalid cannot be seen|
|Keep only failed calls|No need to organize successful samples first|An unconfirmed case is prematurely written as a general rule|
|Record successful and failed calls separately|Both paths need to be maintained|The as-yet-unconfirmed failure behavior must be retained|

We decided to adopt the last option. The scope of this decision is narrow: the test material must accommodate one successful call and one failed call, preserving a visible result for each; it does not declare that the fifth week is valid in all months, nor that the fifth week is always invalid. The scope is deliberately limited to the recording method because it was already clear at the time that the output could not be reproduced reliably, while the final form of the failed call had not yet been settled.

The review entry point is at `tests/calendars/test_gregorian.py`. The only adjacent relationship directly visible at the start of the file is this:

```python
from datetime import date
from unittest import TestCase
from holidays.calendars.gregorian import (
```

This content places the date object, test base class, and Gregorian import in the same place, which is sufficient as an entry point for regression review. Previously, someone wanted to infer implementation ownership from the test file's location; that judgment was not included in the decision. What is needed here is a place to verify inputs and results, not to redraw the implementation modules.

The reverse-counted fourth week remains a necessary reference, but using it as a reference does not mean falling back to it. In the record, `-4` can identify the fourth week counted backward from month-end, and `-5` can identify the fifth week counted backward from month-end. Both have the counting direction in common; that does not make them the same request. In particular, when reviewing the failed call, because `-5` did not produce the expected result, it must not be silently replaced with `-4` and the latter's date treated as the answer to the original request.

To keep this relationship from being flattened into prose in later reading, the current page retains the following state diagram. The diagram does not express the result for any particular month; it only expresses the two types of call material that this record must retain:

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Reverse-counted fifth-week request
    Reverse-counted fifth-week request --> Successful call
    Reverse-counted fifth-week request --> Failed call
```

The role of a successful call is not to prove that the fifth week has unconditional general-purpose capability. It shows that at least one actual call was not prematurely collapsed into another week ordinal before it was recorded. The role of a failed call is likewise not to prove that all fifth-week requests are invalid. It shows that, within the review scope, a path that cannot be reproduced reliably must still appear with its own result and cannot be covered over by a successful sample.

These two types of records should preserve their respective input contexts. The successful side needs to make clear to readers that it truly came from a fifth-week request, not the result of a fourth-week or forward-counted-week request. The failed side needs to show that it is related to the same issue, not an unrelated test interruption. Existing material does not specify whether the failure is an empty result, an assertion mismatch, or some other manifestation, so this page does not presuppose specific wording, nor turn it into a uniform interface contract.

The initial draft once leaned toward "the fifth week may not have a corresponding date, so it should first be treated as invalid." This sentence no longer serves as a basis for the decision. Its problem is not that it is conservative, but that it prematurely fixes a phenomenon still awaiting review as a rule. If it is initially written as always invalid, a later successful call will look like an exception; if it is initially written as always valid, a failed call will instead look like a problem with the test itself. Both formulations obscure the boundary that actually needs to be maintained.

Likewise, we did not adopt the path of "converting the fifth week to a forward week ordinal and then validating it." On the surface, this makes comparison simpler, but it loses the direction expressed by the original request. Later readers can see only a forward-counted week's date and cannot determine whether that date still corresponds to the original reverse-counted fifth week. No second month-week calculation needs to be created for the tests; preserving the correspondence between the original reverse-counted ordinal and the result is sufficient.

Later, the review material added an explicit time dimension. After the handoff was confirmed, the issue was not considered complete; the public record still retained the "one unconfirmed item" notice, and only afterward did actual review begin. This sequence is worth retaining in the decision because it distinguishes three things that are easy to conflate: someone taking over, someone starting the check, and the semantics being determined. The first two have already happened; the third cannot be substituted by them.

CAL-211 is the navigation back to this issue. The card requires the visible results of "Gregorian Reverse Fifth-Week Validity" in one successful call and one failed call to be recorded separately. This requirement matches this page's decision, but the card does not carry the full explanation of fifth-week semantics. Readers need to cross-check between the test entry point and this page: the card identifies the gap, the test preserves the calls and results, and this page explains why neither side can be omitted.

The responsibility boundary is narrowed accordingly. Test records are responsible for pinning down the reverse-counted fifth-week request and the two types of results; Gregorian month-week calculation is responsible for producing the behavior that request actually yields; readers at the interface layer are responsible for confirming that the result has not been written as another week ordinal. Holiday definitions need not participate in the determination here, and date rules from other calendars are not brought in as corroborating evidence. Even if they share date objects, they are not the basis of this decision.

DOC-23 covers Gregorian Reverse Week-Number Cross-Month Results, and can be consulted as adjacent material. The relationship between the two pages must not be reversed. Cross-month results concern the boundary position shown after a call; this page first fixes whether the fifth-week request still has independent successful and failed records. If the cross-month discussion is directly used to replace the validity record, readers will not be able to tell whether they are discussing where the result lands or whether the fifth-week request was rewritten ahead of time.

During review, first check whether the request still uses `-5`, then check whether the adjacent `-4` is retained only as a reference. Then separately confirm that the successful and failed calls each have a readable result. This order comes from confusion that has arisen previously in this issue: sometimes a failure was misread as no test having been run, and sometimes the fifth week was quietly turned into the fourth week, leaving only a date that looked reasonable. Checking the input first, then both results, avoids treating these two cases as the same fix.

This update does not invent a specific date, nor specify an exception type for the failed call. The existing record supports only the minimum requirement that success and failure be retained separately; it does not support generalizing either result into a fixed return form. The unconfirmed parts still include the eventual form the failed call will take in the test and which preconditions it shares with the successful call. Until confirmed, no general exception contract should be added based on this page.

If a later change causes the previously failed call to produce a date, first confirm that the request is still the original reverse-counted fifth-week request, then determine whether the month-week calculation actually changed. Conversely, if the previously successful call can no longer produce its original result, do not immediately withdraw `-5` wholesale. Both changes should first return to the test entry to verify that the input, call, and result still correspond to one another. This is the value of recording the fifth and fourth weeks separately: it can show whether the change occurred in the boundary judgment or in the process of rewriting the request.

The current decision remains unchanged: retain `-5` as an independent reverse-counted fifth-week request; do not substitute it with the result of `-4`; retain one successful call and one failed call side by side in the regression material; before the failure behavior is confirmed, do not expand the issue into a uniform exception rule.

# Gregorian Reverse Week Numbering Proposal

This proposal originated from API verification for the multi-region coordination version. The issue at the time was not to add another calendar entry point, but to clarify what Gregorian week-of-month numbers mean on boundary dates. The earliest draft focused on whether "reverse numbering could land back in the input month." That framing was convenient for laying out samples, but it mixed the returned date with the basis for counting weeks, and was not continued for API decisions.

The test entry remains `tests/calendars/test_gregorian.py`. The file header exposes only a few adjacent references: `from datetime import date`, `from unittest import TestCase`, and the calendar imports beginning at `holidays.calendars.gregorian`. This is already where date-based assertions are written, so the trial should sit near the existing tests rather than creating a separate helper layer that converts month sequence numbers into strings. That helper layer would first choose an interpretation on the implementation's behalf, then use its own result to prove itself; it does not help with cross-month samples.

## Wording Left by the Original Draft

The initial draft listed the start of January's third week, the start of January's fourth week, the start of September's fifth week, and the start of August's final week as four candidate groups. Its arrangement had one deliberately conservative aspect: forward week-number samples within the same month were used only to establish observation points, not to derive reverse numbers. The reverse fourth week and reverse fifth week each need an independent record, because `-4` and `-5` are not synonymous ways of writing adjacent parameters.

The original recommendation was to record only the final day value next to each sample. That approach remains in the old section, but is no longer sufficient. An isolated day value cannot show at which point between the input month, selected week, and returned date the boundary was crossed; when August's final week meets the following month, the reader also cannot tell whether this is a date display issue or a week-number interpretation issue. As a result, the old draft could easily mislabel "result not in the input month" as a failure.

## Record Dates, Not In-Month Assertions

For the follow-up trial, record three things for each candidate sample: the target month at call time, the supplied week number, and the actual date returned. If the result needs to be displayed, split the date into month and day, but do not require in advance that the month field equal the target month. This makes crossing months no longer a filter before the assertion, but an observable result.

The two January sample groups must be placed side by side. They are used to check whether the starts of the third and fourth weeks are interpreted using the same counting method. September's fifth week must not be used only as proof that a fifth week exists; it should be kept separate from the reverse fifth week to avoid mistaking the availability of a forward number for the reverse number necessarily being valid. August's final week is only for observing the boundary and should not be generalized into a conclusion about the end of every month.

This also changes how day values are recorded. If candidate output contains any of 15, 19, 22, 23, or 29, the test should retain them as the date portion of that sample, rather than concatenating these numbers into a rule that holds across months. Different months may produce the same day value; the same month may return different dates for different week numbers. The draft's original plan to "deduplicate by day value" should be dropped.

## Two Options

**Approach A: Add explicit date samples to the existing test class.** Each assertion directly specifies the month, week number, and expected date. The benefit is that a failure output immediately shows the concrete boundary, and it sits next to the existing use of `date`. The cost is that the number of samples grows with the boundaries, and one loop cannot summarize all months.

**Approach B: Write a generated sweep first, then select the months that fail.** This can quickly scan more combinations, but its output conflates discovering a date with whether the public API should promise that date. For this proposal, which discusses only cross-month results, the sweep output can serve as private verification material but cannot directly replace readable regression samples.

Retain Approach A as the trial direction. This decision does not assert that all reverse weeks should cross months, nor that crossing months is always correct; it only keeps the assessment of each selected sample in a date assertion that can be rechecked. Approach B has not been removed because, if boundary patterns later prove inconsistent across months, it will still be needed to locate candidate months.

## Stop Conditions

Withdraw the trial if any of the following occurs: first, the new assertions force the Gregorian tests to change the entry point for existing date queries; second, the sample passes only after in-month filtering; third, the same input depends on test execution order even though no calendar rules have changed. If any of these occurs, do not keep adding more months; return to interpreting week starts and month-end attribution.

By contrast, a result crossing into the adjacent month is not, by itself, a reason to withdraw. It only means that the sample needs to display both the target month and the actual date. The migration cost is small: the old in-month samples can remain; they only need to be rewritten from "in-month results" to "date results for a given month and number."

## Still Open

This addendum only records that the materials were reviewed; it does not include new test run records. Therefore, this page still cannot determine which candidate group ultimately enters the regression set or whether reverse week five has an available result in every month. Nor is there material supporting direct generalization of these Gregorian observations to other calendar implementations.

CAL-212 remain the entry point for follow-up verification. Their task description calls for reproducing the cross-month result of reverse week numbering from the pre-call state and confirming whether any additional visible changes remain after completion; until that result is available, this page remains only a record of the old approach and sample organization, not the current API definition.

# National and Financial Calendar Export Migration Process

The earliest route treated `holidays/financial/shenzhen_stock_exchange.py` as the investigation starting point. This file was not treated as implementation documentation for the public export; rather, the issue name and call name led people to the financial directory. During later reviews, it was still opened first: the file header contains a visible direct dependency.

```python
from holidays.financial.shanghai_stock_exchange import ShanghaiStockExchange
```

The migration record retains this line so that anyone tracing back knows what the old path reveals immediately: a Shanghai Stock Exchange class name appears next to the Shenzhen file. It is suitable for confirming adjacency in the financial directory, but not for replacing consumer records. The fact that the national calendar and financial calendar can be obtained from the public export is the target of this compatibility check; as for which module a given consumer imports from and which fields it retrieves, that must be confirmed in the consumer's code and actual returned content.

```text
Before switch                              After switch
────────────────────────────────────────────────
Call site ──old entry──> Shenzhen financial calendar file      Call site ──> Country and Financial Calendar Public Exports
                    │                                      │
                    └─> ShanghaiStockExchange               └─> Result for same date

Old path retained for comparison; call sites and results are recorded for each migration batch.
```

## First, make the migration target explicit

"Country and Financial Calendar Public Exports" is not simply a matter of writing two directory names side by side in the caller. Before switching, a call site must first identify whether it needs the national calendar, the exchange calendar, or both. If it only reads market closing dates, use the financial-calendar result for comparison; if it displays a country's holidays, use the national-calendar result for comparison. The two uses can occur on the same product page, but the migration record should not share one sample without distinguishing the type.

The first batch should be selected by call site, not by file count. It must be possible to see the old entry, pin down a date input, and obtain the returned content before and after the switch. This way, even if the public-export side shows a difference, you can return to a specific call site to handle it. Anyone who sees only `shenzhen_stock_exchange.py` should first record that file and its direct import; do not use that alone to place all financial-calendar consumers under the Shenzhen Stock Exchange.

At minimum, the record should retain four items: the call site, the pre-switch entry, the selected calendar object, and the old result for the same date. Here, "result" includes the content the caller actually uses; if the caller displays names, it cannot save only the date set; if the caller branches by calendar category, retain which side it selected. Without these details, file-level reading can only show where the investigation started; it cannot support a determination that the consumer migration is complete.

## How to handle the first batch

The first batch handles only one call site. Before switching, preserve the old entry, do not change its parameter conventions, and do not opportunistically tidy up surrounding national- or financial-calendar code. Take a date already used by the call site and save the old result; then change only the import or retrieval location to the public export and use the same date. The comparison should follow the consumer's purpose: when it depends on dates, inspect dates; when it displays names, inspect names; when it distinguishes categories, inspect categories.

If all three types of content appear at the same call site, the comparison order still begins with object selection. First confirm whether the national calendar or financial calendar was obtained, then inspect the dates, and finally the name or display text. This avoids misrecording "a reasonable result from another type of calendar was obtained" as "the original calendar's content changed." The public export solves consistency of the acquisition entry; it does not automatically eliminate the semantic differences between the national calendar and the exchange calendar.

Once the first batch passes, select call sites that use the same entry. Here, "same entry" means that their original way of obtaining the calendar was the same, not that the file path was in the same directory. One call site may directly care about the financial calendar, while another may read the national calendar alongside it in the same feature; the latter should be listed as the next batch so that two object selections are not mixed into one difference.

## Do not keep only screenshot conclusions as comparison evidence

The pre-switch content is what is most easily lost from old records. During migration, leave reviewable values or test output beside the call site, and note the date and calendar selection. Writing "Results are consistent" is insufficient for handling later regression, because people later will not know whether the comparison was of names, dates, or object categories. Conversely, there is no need to copy the results for the entire calendar directory here; each batch should save only the portion actually used by that call site.

Names must be compared as-is. If a name after the public export is replaced with an empty value, another language, or an extra marker, the consumer may still obtain the date but show a user-visible difference. Dates must also be recorded separately: the same name does not mean the calendar objects are the same, and the same dates cannot prove that the category has not changed. This separation is for locating migration differences, not for requiring every call site to display all fields.

For a call site that reads both national and financial results, it is recommended to perform two independent comparisons first, and then decide whether to merge the display at the UI layer. First compare the old and new national-calendar results; once that is complete, compare the financial-calendar pair. If the two sources are directly combined into one date list, when omissions or duplicates appear it is difficult to determine whether they were caused by the public export, the caller's merge logic, or the original data-retrieval range.

## How long to retain the old path

The old file is not the sole source for every migration batch. Its value is that financial-calendar investigation can still follow `holidays/financial/shenzhen_stock_exchange.py` back to `ShanghaiStockExchange`, the visible adjacency. Callers actually using other national calendars or other financial calendars should still preserve their own pre-switch entries. Forcing all old results to use the Shenzhen file as the baseline would make unrelated callers lose their original comparison object.

Therefore, during the switch, do not schedule deletion of the old entry, and do not rewrite the old path as an alias of the public export to create superficial consistency. The old entry should remain until the call sites in that batch have completed their comparisons and the differences have been explained or reverted. This allows public-export issues and changes made by the caller itself to be traced separately; when someone later traces through the financial directory, the original clues will not be lost because of a migration.

The old-path record can be short: the file path, the visible direct import, and which comparison batch it serves. Do not infer unverified aggregation relationships from these three items. The actual caller records related to the public export should be placed under the batch item; at minimum, they should let the next review locate the original entry and the same date.

## Recovery after discovering differences

When a difference appears, first restore the current call site to the pre-switch entry; do not roll back other call sites that have already been migrated just because one consumer's result differs. After restoring it, read the same date again; if the old result returns, retain the old result, new result, and call site, and wait for a review focused on the public export. If it still differs after restoration, first check whether the call site also changed the object selection, date source, or result processing, and then continue investigating.

Do not handle the following situations together: the national calendar is missing a date, the financial calendar has an extra date, the displayed name changed, and the category selection changed. All of them may appear as "the holiday on the page is wrong," but the routes for tracing them back are different. When recording them, state whether the current call site takes the national or financial calendar, and whether the difference occurred in the date, name, or category. This way, after restoring the old entry, the next switch can redo only the affected step.

If the difference appears only in the consumer's display layer, restoring the old entry does not mean that the public export itself has been disproved; conversely, different content returned by the public export should not be concealed by modifying the display layer. First retain both sides' results, then determine whether the import path, calendar selection, or the caller's subsequent processing needs review. Do not record one restoration here as a failure of the entire batch migration; what is restored is one specific call site.

## First consumer record still to be added

The pending item left by CAL-214 is: find a caller still using "Country and Financial Calendar Public Exports", and verify its actual version, entry, and current result. This record has not yet been replaced by the old file path. Once found, first record it as a separate batch: what the old entry was, where the public export replaced it, which date was fixed, and what content the caller actually read.

After that, decide whether it belongs to the national-calendar batch or the financial-calendar batch; if it involves both, split it into two comparisons.
